source: Hitchcock, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Critical Thinking' sec. 12.1 (reports McPeck 1981, Critical Thinking and Education)
finding: McPeck argued there are no general thinking skills, because thinking is always about some subject matter. Schools should teach thinking inside subjects, not as a separate course. Critics (Paul 1985, Siegel 1985) say writing and speaking are general abilities that are always about some subject, so his argument needs more.
numbers: No numbers. McPeck held a strong thesis (conceptual subject-specificity of abilities) and exempted the disposition to suspend judgment, which he called general.
limits: Philosophical claim, not an experiment. Counter-example: the ability to spot confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions.
agent_relevance: The strong claim (nothing is general) is too strong. The agent should keep a small set of general checks but key most lessons to problem class.

source: Hitchcock, SEP 'Critical Thinking' sec. 12.1 (reports Ennis 1989 and three kinds of specificity)
finding: Three versions of subject-specificity: conceptual (logically true), epistemological (norms of good thinking differ by field), empirical (a good thinker in one field is not automatically good in another). Ennis answered that 'field' is vague and that inter-field principles exist, e.g. hypothetico-deductive reasoning. Only the empirical version raises the transfer problem.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: A more modest thesis, also endorsed by McPeck, is epistemological subject-specificity
limits: SEP says evidence that cross-domain instruction aids transfer is scanty and calls for well-designed studies of the conditions that favour transfer.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact question to test: lessons keyed by class, but does a lesson from class A help class B (empirical specificity)? Measure it, do not assume it.

source: Hitchcock, SEP 'Critical Thinking' sec. 12.1 (common ground of the debate)
finding: Both sides agree that critical thinking about any topic needs background knowledge about it. Hypothetico-deductive skill is no use without knowing what explanations are plausible.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Statement of common ground, not a test.
agent_relevance: Domain facts are a precondition. A schema that carries only abstract rules with no domain store will not transfer value.

source: Thorndike & Woodworth (1901) The influence of improvement in one mental function upon the efficiency of other functions, Psych Review 8:247-261
finding: Founding experiment for common-elements theory. Subjects trained to estimate areas (with error feedback). Gains did not spread evenly to estimating other shapes, and some individuals showed no spread at all. The authors concluded that spread of practice happens only where identical elements are shared by the trained and the tested function.
numbers: Test series: areas of different shapes and sizes, before and after training. Table values were lost in the HTML copy, so no exact errors recorded. Subject count not read.
quote: spread of practice occurs only where identical elements are concerned in the influencing and influenced function
limits: Tiny samples of a few trained adults; no modern statistics. The authors note a habit such as discounting one's own error is itself an identical element that can transfer.
agent_relevance: Transfer follows shared elements. Tag lessons with surface and structural features of the problem class and apply them where those features match.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), summarising Thorndike 1923 and Broyler, Thorndike & Woodyard 1924
finding: Thorndike tested formal discipline (Latin or geometry make you think better) with school tests in autumn and spring. Students who took the supposedly mind-training courses did not gain more. The results did not support formal discipline.
numbers: No effect sizes in the source text.
limits: Methods were criticised (Rosenblatt 1967). Secondhand; primary not opened.
agent_relevance: Prior art for 'hard content gives no free general benefit'. Do not expect gains from one class to lift others without a shared element.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Gick & Holyoak (1980, 1983) tumour and fortress analogy
finding: Subjects given Duncker's tumour-ray problem rarely solved it in 20 minutes. Others read the fortress story first, which contained the solution, and still mostly failed to use it. Merely saying the story might help raised solution rates to nearly 100 per cent. Using the analogy was easy; noticing to use it was the failure.
numbers: Time limit 20 minutes. With hint, 'nearly 100 per cent' (source wording). Group sizes and exact other percentages not in this source.
quote: Merely mentioning that the story might help boosted solution rates to nearly 100 per cent.
limits: Secondhand summary of the primary papers; primary numbers not opened by me.
agent_relevance: Core point: the failure is a retrieval cue problem, not a skill problem. Memory needs retrieval keyed to deep structure, or a program-side prompt that says a stored lesson may apply.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Jepson, Krantz & Nisbett (1983) on the law of large numbers
finding: People grasp that 20 dice throws beat two in a randomness setting, but do not use sample size when judging a person from two maths tests or a brief look at friendliness. A principle learned in one setting stays encapsulated.
numbers: No percentages in this source.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: A general rule stored without class tags will not fire in an unfamiliar surface form. Store each rule with examples from several surfaces.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (1999) problem comparison
finding: Business students compared two negotiation stories with different surface and the same contract solution. Two weeks later they used that solution more on a novel problem than students who only read the stories.
numbers: Delay 2 weeks. Exact rates not in this source.
limits: Secondhand; Kurtz, Boukrina & Gentner 2013 cited as the same method.
agent_relevance: Strongest practical lever for transfer found here: compare two solved cases that differ in surface. The program can do this: when storing a lesson, merge it with an earlier lesson of a different class and keep the shared part.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Catrambone (1995, 1998) subgoal labels
finding: Students who label solution steps with the goal each step serves handle changed problems better than students taught lock-step procedures (for example work problems with a small twist).
numbers: No numbers in this source.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Store operators with the purpose of each step, not only the steps. Supports an operator record with a goal field.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Scherer, Siddiq & Viveros (2018) meta-analysis of programming transfer
finding: Learning to program transfers to creative thinking, maths, metacognition, spatial skills and reasoning. Effects were considerably smaller with an active control group, and there was no benefit for literacy, which points to conceptual overlap rather than general training.
numbers: Average g = .47 overall (source text).
limits: Placebo and active-control confound. The active-control value is not given in the source.
agent_relevance: Transfer tracks conceptual overlap. Expect gains between classes that share structure and nothing elsewhere.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), reporting Helsdingen et al. (2010), Royal Netherlands Navy
finding: Officers were taught a step sequence for analysing tactical problems, then 8 hours of simulator training with expert feedback. They outperformed controls on a new surface-warfare problem and on air-warfare problems.
numbers: 8 hours of training; judges rated contingency plans. Effect size not in source.
limits: Secondhand. Near to mid transfer (same discipline).
agent_relevance: A taught step sequence plus practice with feedback gives within-field transfer. Fits a per-class operator sequence with feedback.

source: Willingham (2019) How to teach critical thinking (NSW Education), on general critical-thinking programmes (Ritchhart & Perkins 2005; Kozulin et al. 2010)
finding: School add-on programmes of about 5 hours a week for one or two years seldom test real transfer: puzzle training is measured by puzzles, debate training by argument tests. Where transfer was tested, results were absent or modest and faded quickly.
numbers: No effect sizes in source.
quote: positive results have been absent or modest and quick to fade
limits: Narrative review by one author.
agent_relevance: Beware benchmarks that match the training. Measure transfer on held-out classes, never on the class the lesson came from.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically, Rev Educ Res 85:275-314, read via Clearing House Unterricht summary
finding: Overall effect of critical-thinking instruction is small and stable across education level, subject matter and duration. Tests tied to the content taught improved more than generic tests.
numbers: Overall g = 0.30 over 341 effect sizes (summary says 'studies'). Content-specific CT g = 0.57 (97). Disposition g = 0.23 (25). Subject facts g = 0.33 (140).
limits: I opened the summary, not the full paper. 341 is likely effect sizes, not independent studies. Mostly near-transfer outcomes.
agent_relevance: Small generic gain, bigger gain for content-tied tests: consistent with class-keyed lessons.

source: Abrami et al. (2015), read via Clearing House Unterricht summary: moderators
finding: Teaching abstract principles explicitly and then applying them to concrete topics worked best. Combining application-oriented instruction, dialogue and mentoring gave the largest effect. Explicit versus infused teaching did not differ significantly.
numbers: Combined three approaches g = 0.57 (19 studies). Problem solving g = 0.35 (31). Role-playing g = 0.61 (5). Teacher questions g = 0.38 (19). Whole-class guided discussion g = 0.42 (16). Small group g = 0.41 (14).
limits: Few studies in the best cells. Short interventions (1 hour to 2 days) still gave significant effects.
agent_relevance: Principle plus varied concrete cases beats either alone. Store each lesson as a principle plus examples from several classes.

source: Abrami et al. (2008) Instructional interventions affecting critical thinking skills and dispositions: Stage 1 meta-analysis (figures from a search snippet only; the paper returned 403)
finding: Earlier stage of the same meta-analysis found a similar small-to-moderate average effect.
numbers: 117 studies, 20,698 participants, 161 effects, mean g+ = 0.341 (snippet only).
limits: Not opened; page returned 403.
agent_relevance: Shows the 2015 figure is stable across two analyses by the same group.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training, Curr Dir Psychol Sci 26:515-520
finding: Three meta-analyses of experiments in children found small to moderate overall effects that shrank to near zero with active control groups. Near transfer (WM training to other memory tasks) held. The authors conclude far transfer rarely occurs.
numbers: Overall g: chess 0.34, music 0.16, WM training 0.12. Music vs passive control 0.25 (k=64), vs active control 0.03 (k=54). WM training passive 0.18 (k=34), active 0.05 (k=40). WM training on memory tasks: 0.44 (active) and 0.46 (passive).
quote: far transfer of learning rarely occurs
limits: Typically developing children. Chess had only one active-control study (0.10). Critics dispute how controls and moderators were coded.
agent_relevance: Hard evidence that general-skill training does not lift unrelated skills. Supports not sharing operator lessons across classes by default.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017), theory section on common elements, chunking and template theory
finding: Common-elements theory (Thorndike & Woodworth 1901) predicts frequent near transfer and rare far transfer. Chunking and template theory (Chase & Simon 1973; Gobet & Simon 1996) say expertise rests on tens of thousands of domain chunks, hence little transfer. General abilities (intelligence, WM) predict success, but training them does not carry over.
numbers: Chess players' cognitive ability exceeds non-players by about 0.5 SD (Sala et al. 2017). Burgoyne et al. 2016 report correlations of chess skill with fluid intelligence, speed, WM and comprehension knowledge.
limits: Correlation is not a training effect; able people self-select into chess and music.
agent_relevance: Domain chunk stores explain most expert skill. The agent's per-class memory is the analogue of chunks.

source: Fu, Zhou, Yuan & Cai (2026) The asymmetry of working memory training transfer, Psychon Bull Rev 33:227
finding: Transfer between trained tasks is directional. Updating training transferred to span tasks, but span training did not transfer to updating tasks. Cognitive demand, not only similarity, shapes transfer.
numbers: 55 studies, 208 effect sizes, N = 3,492. Updating to span g = 0.176 (p < .001). Span to updating g = 0.048 (p = .453). Larger at low training doses, in non-adults, with verbal stimuli.
limits: Task-level transfer, not school skills. Effects small.
agent_relevance: Transfer can be one-way: a lesson from a harder class may help an easier class but not the reverse. Log the direction of reuse.

source: Gabriel & Mushtaq (2026) No evidence of transfer of learning between problem-solving tasks using different transformation rules, Open Mind 10:261-286
finding: Four days of training on one string-transformation taskset improved solution rate, efficiency and decision speed on that set. There was no reliable gain on the untrained set beyond direct practice in the probe blocks, although a reusable state-value heuristic existed. This goes against the heuristic-search model's transfer prediction and fits pattern-action association.
numbers: 73 participants completed all sessions (Prolific, ages 22-40); 17 were excluded for failing task checks (8 in group A, 9 in group B), so 56 analysed. Four sessions, each two blocks of 12 problems plus a WM block.
limits: Absence of evidence is not proof; authors list interference, working-memory load and mechanism change as alternatives. Online sample.
agent_relevance: Even when a rule-independent heuristic could be reused, people did not reuse it. Do not count on the model to reuse abstract value estimates; supply the matching lesson explicitly.

source: Gabriel & Mushtaq (2026) Open Mind, introduction: the two computational models
finding: Two computational accounts make opposite predictions. Pattern recognition with state-action associations allows only limited transfer to tasks with different actions. Heuristic search with a learned state-value estimate can reuse learning across tasks.
numbers: No numbers; the contrast is tested in the four-day training study (previous line).
limits: The data favoured limited transfer, but alternatives remain.
agent_relevance: Formal model: lessons are action-bound unless the value function is reusable. Treat stored lessons as state-action pairs and key them by class.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nat Hum Behav (arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat undergraduates on text matrix and analogy tasks, but on story analogies it was clearly worse than students, especially for far (cross-domain) analogy. GPT-4 did better in a preliminary check.
numbers: Story analogy, humans N=54: far analogy t(53)=16.7. GPT-3 near analogy p=0.0039 but far analogy p=0.065 (not significant). Humans beat GPT-3 (OR=0.37, p=0.0003). 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story on every trial. Digit matrices: 40 humans; verbal and string analogies N=57.
limits: GPT-3 only; GPT-4 results preliminary. Contamination and robustness of the matrix results have been questioned elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as people: near analogy is easy, far analogy is hard. Far-analog retrieval should not be left to the model.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023), Gick & Holyoak replication with GPT-3
finding: Asked the tumour problem alone, GPT-3 proposed injecting the radiation source into the tumour. After reading the general story first it identified the convergence solution. So the model uses a supplied analogy.
numbers: Qualitative, one problem, no counts (Supplementary S5.1).
limits: Single case; the famous problem may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Matches the human pattern: use is easy once the analog is supplied. Supports supplying the stored lesson from code.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Counterfactual tasks, NAACL (arXiv 2307.02477)
finding: Eleven tasks, each with a counterfactual version of the same rule (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, rotated drawing coordinates, altered guitar tuning, and others). GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and other models including PaLM-2 did worse on counterfactuals, though above chance. Models lean on narrow, default-condition procedures.
numbers: GPT-3.5 parseable drawing programs fell from 99% (default) to 62%, 71% and 75% for vertical flip, 90-degree and 180-degree rotation. Gap was smaller when the counterfactual was common (bases 8 and 16 easier than 9 and 11).
limits: Chain-of-thought and few-shot prompts only partly closed the gap; per-task scores not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Skills are tied to the form seen in training. Lessons should state the conditions in which they were learned.

source: Zhao et al. (2026, v6) Is chain-of-thought reasoning of LLMs a mirage? A data distribution lens (arXiv 2508.01191)
finding: Models trained from scratch in a controlled environment (DataAlchemy) show chain-of-thought only as an in-distribution pattern. Shifts in task, length or format break it. For an unseen transformation, models followed the nearest seen transformation, giving right reasoning with wrong answers or the reverse.
numbers: Exact match 100% in distribution; 0.01% for a new composition; 0% for partly and fully out of distribution. Models 62K to 3B parameters trained from scratch; also LLaMA3-8B and Qwen3-14B tests.
limits: Small synthetic setting, not frontier models. A generalisation bound (Theorem 3.1) ties error to the distribution gap.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal model of transfer: error grows with the gap between training class and test class. Argues for class keys and for flagging when a case is far from stored ones.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does math reasoning improve general LLM capabilities? Understanding transferability of LLM reasoning (arXiv 2507.00432)
finding: Over 20 open reasoning models tuned for maths: most gains did not carry to other reasoning or non-reasoning tasks. In controlled runs on Qwen3-14B-Base with only maths data, reinforcement learning (GRPO) transferred while supervised fine-tuning mostly did not and often lost general ability.
numbers: RL model: 55.7% AIME24, 87.8% MATH500, 33.8% OlympiadBench; RL beat the SFT model by 17.1% on LiveCodeBench2 and 1.8% on GPQA (SFT GPQA 55.9%). Transferability Index = z-normalised gain over base, per task group.
limits: One base model in the controlled study; recipe and data are partly confounded. The index is the authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: Training choice decides transfer. A scaffold has no training, so gains come from what is stored and retrieved; test each lesson on other classes.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning, ICLR (arXiv 2409.12183)
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. Chain-of-thought gives large gains on maths and logic and almost none elsewhere. On MMLU the gain is almost all on questions with an equals sign.
numbers: Average gain: symbolic 14.2, maths 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without; other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. Gains up to 66.9 (GSM8K) and 41.6 (MATH).
limits: Prompted CoT only; tool use beat CoT on symbolic execution.
agent_relevance: A thinking operator pays off only in some problem classes. Strong support for class-keyed operator selection.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and fate: limits of transformers on compositionality, NeurIPS (arXiv 2305.18654)
finding: On multi-digit multiplication, logic grid puzzles and dynamic programming, transformers appear to match linearised subgraphs seen in training rather than learn systematic procedures. Accuracy decays quickly as the computation graph deepens.
numbers: ChatGPT 55% and GPT-4 59% on 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication.
limits: Other tables not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Transfer to deeper or longer cases of the same class fails; the program should verify long cases with code.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The illusion of thinking (arXiv 2506.06941)
finding: Reasoning models handle puzzle size well up to a point, then collapse to zero accuracy. Skill in one puzzle does not predict a sibling: a model near perfect on Tower of Hanoi with 5 disks failed River Crossing at size 3.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) near perfect; River Crossing N=3 (11 moves) failed. Three regimes: simple (non-thinking better), medium (thinking better), high (both collapse).
limits: Controlled puzzles; critics say output-length limits explain some of the collapse.
agent_relevance: Success in one class says little about a sibling class with similar logic. Do not share operator success rates across classes without tests.

source: Ruis et al. (2025) Procedural knowledge in pretraining drives reasoning in large language models, ICLR (arXiv 2411.12580)
finding: Influence-function analysis of 2.5B pretraining tokens for 7B and 35B models. Factual answers rely on distinct documents per question, but reasoning questions of the same task share influential documents that hold procedures (formulae, code). Reasoning looks like a reusable procedure per task, not retrieval.
numbers: Three simple maths reasoning tasks; models 7B and 35B; 2.5B tokens.
limits: Influence approximations; simple tasks; correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-class procedure: items of a class share a procedure, so a stored procedure per class is the right unit.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners (arXiv 2503.01307)
finding: Verification, backtracking, subgoal setting and backward chaining predict whether a model improves under RL. Priming Llama with these behaviours, even in incorrect solutions, matched Qwen. Behaviour presence mattered more than answer correctness.
numbers: Countdown game: Qwen-2.5-3B reached about 60% accuracy vs Llama-3.2-3B about 30% under identical RL.
limits: One game, 3B models; may not hold on open tasks.
agent_relevance: Some operator-level behaviours are generic enough to prime across problems. A hint that a small general set (as McPeck conceded for dispositions) is worth keeping.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agent Workflow Memory (arXiv 2409.07429)
finding: Workflows induced from past web tasks help on new tasks, new websites and new domains, and gains grow as the train-test gap widens.
numbers: Mind2Web step success with GPT-4: cross-task 36.2 (MindAct) to 45.1 (offline AWM) and 43.6 (online); cross-website 30.1 to 33.7 and 33.9; cross-domain 18.6 to 32.6 and 35.5. WebArena: 51.1% relative gain over best published autonomous method; 24.6% relative gain on Mind2Web cross-task.
limits: Whole-task success stays tiny (cross-domain 1.0 baseline vs 0.7 offline and 1.7 online).
agent_relevance: Stored workflows carry across websites and domains in one setting, though whole-task success remains low. Evidence for shared memory with a class key.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (arXiv 2308.10144), transfer experiment
finding: Insights extracted from HotpotQA, adapted by GPT-4 and given with few-shot examples, raised FEVER success over baselines.
numbers: FEVER success rate: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer without task demos 65, ExpeL transfer 70 (percent, small SD).
limits: Source and target both use Wikipedia lookup, so tool and structure are shared (close transfer). Insights were rewritten for the target task.
agent_relevance: Transfer worked when tool and format were shared. Rewrite the lesson for the new class instead of copying it.

source: Synthesis across the sources read in this file
finding: Transfer happens with shared structure and cued retrieval, falls with surface and domain gap, and is easily overstated when controls are weak.
numbers: Active-control effects near zero (music 0.03 vs 0.25 passive); generic CT g = 0.30 vs content-specific g = 0.57 (Abrami).
limits: Synthesis line, no new study. Human and LLM gaps may differ in cause.
agent_relevance: Design: key lessons by problem class, retrieve by structure, keep a few general guards, and validate each cross-class use on held-out items.
